name: Cobalt Green
lede: Cobalt green is a pale, clear green made from cobalt and zinc, discovered in 1780 by Sven Rinmann and loved for its permanence but priced out of most painters' hands.

sections.title: Cobalt, then green
sections.body:
The cobalt in the name is the metal, and the metal's name is a miner's insult. German silver miners blamed the mischievous *kobold*, a mine goblin, for an ore that carried arsenic, poisoned the miners and spoiled the silver they were after [15][8][2]. Agricola in 1556 and Mathesius in 1562 both warned about it [15]. Paterson adds that in Bohemia the pigment was thought to be haunted [2].

The green is a family of names. Cobalt green was also sold as Rinmann's green, after its discoverer, and as zinc green, and the Colour Index lists Gellert green as a variant [4][2]. One source links Swedish green to cobalt green; another gives that name to Scheele's green, so it is safer to leave it out of the family [4]. For the cobalt blues and the cobalt metal behind them, see [[cobalt]].

sections.title: Rinmann's green, 1780
sections.body:
Cobalt green was discovered in 1780 by the Swedish chemist Sven Rinmann [1][2]. That is earlier than cobalt blue, which Louis-Jacques Thénard made in 1802 on the orders of Napoleon's minister Chaptal, who wanted a cheaper substitute for ultramarine [1][9]. Paterson describes Rinmann's color as a bright yellowish green, while the Pigment Compendium files the same name under blue-green [2][4]. The books do not settle which way the hue leaned, and the two descriptions fit a pigment whose recipe varied.

The discovery did not produce a paint at once. Ball says the manufacture was viable only when zinc oxide became readily available, and he places the arrival of cobalt green on the market in the middle of the nineteenth century [1]. Pastoureau writes that it was perfected at the end of the eighteenth century and says it cost a fortune [6]. The disagreement is partly one of definition: a laboratory find in 1780 and a tube on a shop shelf are different events [1][6].

sections.title: What is in the tube
sections.body:
Chemically, cobalt green is a cousin of cobalt blue. In cobalt blue the partner of cobalt is alumina; in cobalt green zinc oxide takes part or all of that place [1][3]. Church in 1901 described making it by adding a cobalt salt to a paste of zinc oxide and water, then drying and firing the mass [3].

The proportions were never fixed. Terry in 1893 reported mixtures of 71.5 to 88 per cent zinc oxide and 11.5 to 19 per cent cobalt oxide, along with traces of phosphoric acid, soda and iron oxide, depending on the maker [3]. Salter's edition of Field in 1869 said that only two to three per cent of cobalt was needed [3]. The Colour Index treats the pigment as a mixture of cobalt zincate and zinc oxide that cannot be written as a single compound [3].

Field in 1835 used the same name for two things, one containing zinc or iron and the other a mix of cobalt blue and chrome yellow [3]. Modern tubes labeled cobalt green are often different again: cobalt titanate spinels with nickel and zinc, which the Colour Index lists as Pigment Green 50 [5]. A label on a tube is therefore a color name and not a recipe.

sections.title: Dear and weak
sections.body:
Church called cobalt green chemically and artistically perfect in 1901: bright, and excellent in permanence [1]. He did not say it was cheap. Ball adds that it had poor opacity and remained costly, as the cobalt pigments generally did [1]. Zerr and Rübencamp in 1906 called it unpopular because of its price [4].

The cheaper rivals were artificial ultramarine greens, perfected in the 1820s by Guimet and Gmelin, and the older copper greens [6]. Painters distrusted the ultramarine greens until the 1880s, and the Customs Officer Henri Rousseau used one for his jungles because it was cheaper than cobalt green and safer than copper greens [6]. [[viridian]] won the same market from a different direction. Coles pairs it with cobalt green as the pair of safe, stable, readily available greens that artists finally gained in the nineteenth century [7].

sections.title: Where the cobalts met the painters
sections.body:
Cobalt green is the least conspicuous of a family that remade the palette. Cobalt blue arrived in 1802, cobalt violet was made in France from 1859, and the yellow called aureolin was synthesized in 1831 but not sold as a pigment until 1861 [1]. Cerulean blue, a cobalt and tin compound, reached artists in the 1860s as watercolor and the 1870s as oil [1][9].

The family is also a trap for the careless. Birren's history assigns cobalt blue to the palette of Rubens, almost two centuries before it existed, which is wrong; Ball uses the slip as a warning about ignoring pigment chemistry [14]. Of the twenty principal pigments Ball counts in Impressionist paintings, he names cobalt blue and viridian but not cobalt green [10]. That absence is no proof of non-use, though it fits a pigment too dear and too weak to be an everyday color [1].

A seventeenth-century curiosity points the other way. Cobalt-based inks were used as invisible ink that turned green when warmed [8].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
The swatch here, #7BC6A0, is a light, clear green [11]. Our library gives it three sources: Ridgway's 1912 plate XIX, an ISCC-NBS 1955 block that names it a light yellowish green, and Maerz & Paul's dictionary of 1930 with a first-recorded date of 1780, the year of Rinmann's discovery [11]. The chart sources therefore lean yellowish, which sides with Paterson rather than with the Compendium's blue-green label [2][4][11].

A real tube of cobalt green varies from one maker to another, as the chemistry above suggests [3]. Treat the swatch as a screen color for a family name, not as the pigment itself [11].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Cobalt green is rare in painting. In our archive of 23,781 paintings it appears in only seven works at one per cent of the canvas within four units of the swatch, and in four at five per cent within six units [12]. It is rarer than 75 per cent of the named colors [12]. As photographed, the four are *Spring on the Range* of 1875, where the color fills 36 per cent of the canvas, and an *Aurora* of 1825 at about 10 per cent [12]. The other two are [[painter:vincent-van-gogh|Van Gogh]]'s *Still Life of Oranges and Lemons with Blue Gloves* of 1889 at about 16 per cent and a portrait by [[painter:edgar-degas|Degas]] of 1879 at about 8 per cent [12].

The earliest of them is 1825, decades before cobalt green is said to have reached the market, so the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph and not evidence of the pigment [12][1]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [12].

In print, the phrase is close to absent from Google Books around 1820, shows up by the 1840s, rises fastest in the 1880s and peaks in the 1910s [13]. The nearest named colors are Neuwieder Green, Medium Aquamarine and Pale Teal [12]. To train the eye, set it between the greener Neuwieder Green and the bluer Medium Aquamarine and notice how narrow its slot is [12].

openers: Cobalt green was found in 1780, twenty-two years before cobalt blue, and then waited decades for a use.
The name is a pigment recipe that never had one fixed recipe: the zinc and cobalt shares varied by maker.
Our archive holds only four paintings with a broad passage of this green.
